title: Crème anglaise
summary: A pourable vanilla custard sauce of milk, cream and egg yolks, cooked gently until it coats a spoon.
steps: Set a bowl inside a larger bowl of ice water and put a fine sieve over it.
Heat the milk and cream in a saucepan until steaming and small bubbles appear at the edge.
Meanwhile whisk the egg yolks, allulose and salt in a bowl until smooth and slightly paler.
Pour about a third of the hot milk into the yolks in a thin stream, whisking, then pour everything back into the pan.

Cook over low heat, stirring constantly with a spatula, until the sauce thickens enough to coat the spatula and a finger drawn through it leaves a clean line, 80–82 °C (176–180 °F). Never let it boil.
Immediately strain it into the chilled bowl, stir in the vanilla, and stir now and then as it cools. Refrigerate, covered, up to 3 days. Serve cold or barely warm.

swaps.note: use coconut milk for both, not coconut cream, or the sauce is too heavy

dairy_free_notes: Made with coconut milk the sauce is slightly thicker and tastes of coconut; it pairs best with tropical fruit and chocolate.
tips: If it starts to curdle, pull it off the heat at once and blend it smooth while still warm.
Churned in an ice cream maker, the same custard becomes a vanilla ice cream base.

origin.history: Crème anglaise means 'English cream', a name usually explained as a nod to the English fondness for pouring custard. Sweetened milk thickened with egg yolks was made in both countries for centuries, and the sauce was a fixture of classical French cookery by the 1800s. It is also the base of many custards and ice creams.
